title: Gemini Evaluation and Observability
summary: This intermediate module enables learners to design a repeatable evaluation for Gemini outputs and connect evaluation results to request observations. After completing it, learners can distinguish output quality from operational behavior, define evidence for each, and investigate a regression without relying on an unspecified tool.
objectives: Define test cases and scoring criteria for evaluating Gemini outputs.
Identify the request observations needed to investigate quality and operational regressions.
Compare a candidate result with a baseline while controlling unrelated changes.
Connect an aggregate evaluation result to individual cases and their recorded request context.

sections.title: Level and scope
paragraphs: This is an intermediate-level module. It assumes that you understand a basic request-response interaction, can read a simple test case, and know that model outputs can vary. It does not assume knowledge of a particular evaluation framework, monitoring product, programming language, or deployment architecture.

In this module, evaluation means applying stated criteria to outputs from defined test cases. Observability means retaining enough request context and outcome information to explain what happened in an individual case and to detect patterns across cases. These working definitions keep the method usable without introducing unsupported product-specific features.

sections.title: Design a repeatable evaluation
paragraphs: Start by writing the task in observable terms. For example, instead of asking whether an output is good, state whether it follows the requested format, includes required information, avoids prohibited content, and remains relevant to the input. Each criterion should describe evidence a reviewer can find in the output.

Create a stable set of test cases that represents the task. Give every case a unique case identifier, its input, and the criteria that apply to it. Include ordinary cases and cases that are difficult for reasons relevant to the task. Do not change the cases while comparing a candidate with a baseline, because changing both the system and the test set prevents a controlled comparison.

Choose a scoring rule before inspecting candidate results. A rule may be a pass or fail decision for each criterion or an ordered rating with a written meaning for every rating. Apply the same rule to the baseline and candidate. Record the case-level decision and the evidence supporting it rather than retaining only an aggregate score.

Aggregate results only after case-level scoring. An aggregate can show that performance changed, but it cannot explain which inputs changed or why. Inspect failed cases and meaningful groups of cases before deciding that a candidate is better or worse.

sections.title: Observe the context around each result
paragraphs: For each evaluated request, associate the case identifier with the input revision, the model identifier selected by the application, the time of the request, the outcome, and the evaluation result. If your application measures duration or categorizes failures, those observations can help separate an output-quality problem from an operational problem.

A quality regression occurs when outputs score worse under the same cases and criteria. An operational regression concerns request behavior such as more failures or longer measured duration. These categories can occur together, but they answer different questions and should not be merged into one unexplained score.

Retain only information that your policies permit. Inputs and outputs can contain sensitive material, so evaluation and observation records should follow the same access, retention, and review rules that apply to the underlying data. This module does not specify a storage product or policy because none is established by the supplied material.

sections.title: Investigate a regression
paragraphs: First, confirm that the baseline and candidate used the same test cases, criteria, and scoring rule. Next, locate the individual cases responsible for the aggregate difference. Compare their recorded context and determine whether the change is concentrated in a particular kind of input, an output criterion, or an operational outcome.

Change one relevant factor at a time when testing a possible explanation. Then rerun the affected cases and the stable evaluation set. This preserves a traceable connection among the observed regression, the proposed cause, and the evidence from the follow-up run.

A useful investigation report states the baseline, candidate, unchanged evaluation conditions, changed factor, affected cases, case-level evidence, and conclusion. If the evidence does not identify a cause, record the cause as UNKNOWN rather than turning a correlation into a factual explanation.

sections.title: A practical workflow
paragraphs: Define the task and criteria, assign stable case identifiers, run a baseline, and retain case-level outputs and context. Run the candidate against the same cases, apply the same scoring rule, compare aggregate and case-level results, and inspect operational observations separately from output-quality scores.

This workflow gives you a capability you did not need to have before the module: you can now construct a controlled Gemini evaluation and use linked request evidence to investigate a regression. The method deliberately avoids naming an implementation tool because the supplied material does not establish one.

questions.prompt: Which result is specifically evidence of an output-quality regression under this module's definitions?
choices: Outputs score worse when the same cases, criteria, and scoring rule are used.
The application records a different request time.
The evaluation contains stable case identifiers.
questions.explanation: A quality regression is a decline in output scores under unchanged evaluation conditions. Request timing is operational context, while case identifiers support traceability.

questions.prompt: What should remain unchanged when comparing a candidate with a baseline?
choices: The test cases, criteria, and scoring rule.
Every output produced by the model.
The conclusion written after the comparison.
questions.explanation: Keeping the cases, criteria, and scoring rule stable makes the comparison controlled. Outputs may differ, and the conclusion must follow the evidence.

questions.prompt: Why should case-level results be retained instead of keeping only an aggregate score?
choices: They show which inputs and criteria contributed to a change.
They guarantee that every candidate is better than the baseline.
They remove the need for predefined scoring criteria.
questions.explanation: An aggregate indicates an overall change, while case-level records provide the evidence needed to locate and investigate that change.

questions.prompt: What should an investigation report say when the evidence does not identify the cause of a regression?
choices: The most correlated observation is the confirmed cause.
questions.explanation: The module requires recording the cause as UNKNOWN when available evidence does not establish it.
